cross_language_consistency_note: Same-level-means-the-same-thing was enforced three ways. (1) One frozen probe requirement per capability, identical in content for all ten languages: the same product type, the same two generic instantiations, the same closure, the same 'héllo' codepoint count of 5, the same sqrt/exp/log/sin/cos values, the same 2^70 or the same INT_MAX+1, the same 99/99 view mutation. Only the build command differs, and it is each language's own frozen recipe from environment.json. (2) Every contestable indicator was resolved by ONE rule written down before Quidra was examined and then applied to all ten: X02 requires either toolchain-checked exhaustiveness over a declared closed alternative set, or a standard-library type whose documented purpose is to hold one of several alternatives with a readable discriminant (std::variant::index() passes); dynamic-type dispatch in a dynamically typed or interface-based language does not, which is why Python and Go fail X02 while C++ passes it. X06 requires a single binding form that binds two or more components of one aggregate value, which is why Go and Quidra fail it while Zig's `const a, const b = tuple` passes. X11 requires the guarantee to be DOCUMENTED, not merely observed, which is why Python fails despite verified constant folding and TypeScript passes on the handbook's const-enum sentence. X13 requires a documented, toolchain-implemented mechanism by which a module declaration is unavailable to an importer through at least one of the language's import forms; this was verified NEGATIVELY for every language (C++ link failure across TUs, Java 'priv() has private access', Kotlin 'cannot access ... it is private in file', Zig "'privFn' is not marked 'pub'", TypeScript TS2459, Python's import * excluding _priv) and Quidra alone fails because its importer successfully called the module's un-annotated function. X16 requires the bound to be ENFORCED by the toolchain, verified by a violation probe; Python's violation ran with exit 0 and no diagnostic, TypeScript's produced TS2741. X22 requires a first-party testing facility shipped in the toolchain distribution that compiles and runs using distribution artifacts alone; a general-purpose assertion primitive not published as a testing facility (C++ assert, Java assert) does not count, while Quidra's test.check/test.equal and Kotlin's shipped kotlin-test assertions both do - deliberately the same ruling for both, so that Quidra is not credited for something Kotlin is denied. (3) After all ten were assigned, every indicator was re-read column-wise: for each of the 24 capabilities the set of passing languages and the set of failing languages were compared against each other, and no two languages with the same observed evidence hold different verdicts on any indicator.
limitations: X13 and X22 could not be expressed as a single-file program in several languages, so the frozen single-file recipe was applied to the two or three source files the capability inherently needs (C++ header+TU, Java package, Go module, TypeScript module pair, Kotlin package, Swift second module, Zig second file, Python package, Quidra imported .qui). The compiler and flags were never changed. This departure is identical for all ten languages.

TypeScript: tsc ships no type declarations for the Node runtime named in TypeScript's own frozen recipe, and @types/node is third-party, so the X18, X19 and X22 probes declare the CommonJS entry point locally rather than importing node: modules by name. No package outside the toolchain distribution (tsc 7.0.2 + node v24.2.0) was installed or used, but a reader should know that `import * as fs from "node:fs"` does NOT type-check first-party-only. This is a real friction point that this metric does not otherwise capture.

Kotlin X20 and X23 rely on JDK classes reached through Kotlin/JVM interop. They are counted as first-party because official_project_table places the OpenJDK project inside Kotlin's official_project_set. A reader who reads 'first-party standard library' as kotlin-stdlib only would score Kotlin 22 instead of 24 - still level 100.

Kotlin X22 is the closest call in the table: kotlin-test ships in the distribution and its assertion API compiles and runs, but its @Test annotation typealiases to a JUnit annotation the distribution does not ship ('unresolved reference Test'), and no test runner ships either, so no test can be DECLARED using the distribution alone. It is counted satisfied only because Quidra's structurally identical test.check/test.equal is also counted satisfied. Denying both gives Kotlin 23 (still 100) and Quidra 10 (still 40).

Quidra X23 is the most generous award in Quidra's column: it was satisfied by `int[] &view = &buf`, a reference to the whole array, because Quidra cannot form a view over a proper sub-range (`&buf[1:3]` -> error[INDEX_ARITY], and `bytes &view = &data[1:3]` likewise). Every other language satisfied X23 with a genuine sub-range view. Withdrawing this award gives Quidra S=10, which is still the Partial (40) band.

C++ was scored under the frozen -std=c++20 recipe. Apple clang 17 on this host also rejects C++20 named modules outright ('export module' -> error: expected template), which is a host/toolchain property; X13 was awarded through the header + unnamed-namespace route instead, so this host limitation did not cost C++ a point. C++26 saturating arithmetic (std::add_sat), which would satisfy X24, is not reachable under the frozen -std=c++20 recipe and was verified absent.

E2 documentation was retrieved in full for the indicators whose verdict turns on a documented guarantee or a documented absence (Python X11, TypeScript X11, C++ X15, Go X06 and X14, Java X20, Rust X20 and X21, Quidra X04/X05/X16/X19/X22). For the uncontested capabilities the E2 anchor is each language's official standard-library reference for the module used; those were not individually re-fetched, and that shortcut was applied identically to all ten languages.

Swift X11 and Zig X05 were decided partly on compiler diagnostics that name an unshipped or experimental feature, which is E1 evidence of absence rather than an E2 statement that the feature does not exist. The same standard of evidence was accepted for Quidra's thirteen failures.
